On Fekete Points for a Real Simplex

Len Bos Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Univesity of Verona Affiliation: Italy Affiliation: E-mail: leonardpeter.bos@univr.it
Abstract

We survey what is known about Fekete points/optimal designs for a simplex in ℝd.\mathbb{R}^{d}. Several new results are included. The notion of Fejér exponenet for a set of interpolation points is introduced.

†† 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: Primary 41A17; Secondary 41A63.†† Key words and phrases: Fekete points, optimal measures, optimal experimental design, simplex.

Dedicated to Prof. Jaap Korevaar on the occasion of his 100th birthday!

In one variable, as is well known, the Chebyshev points provide an excellent set of points for polynomial interpolation of functions defined on the interval K=[−1,1].K=[-1,1]. In several variables the problem of finding analogues of such near optimal interpolation points is much more difficult and each underlying set K⊂ℝdK\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} must be analyzed indvidually. One general approach, that turns out to be rather fruitful, is to consider the so-called Fekete points (see Definition 0.1 below). These turn out to be strongly related to statistical Optimal Designs (cf. Definition 0.3) and to a property proved first by Fejér [7] (cf. Defintion 0.2)in the interval case. In this work we survey what is known about Fekete points for the case of K⊂ℝd,K\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, a simplex. Some new results are obtained and we introduce the notion of Fejér exponent for a set of interpolation points. We remark that also in the univariate complex case, K⊂ℂ,K\subset\mathbb{C}, Fekete points and their properties have been much studied, including by Prof. J. Korevaar [11], (and the references therein), to whom this paper is dedicated.

Consider then a set of d+1d+1 points Xd:={𝐕1,⋯,𝐕d+1}⊂ℝdX_{d}:=\{{\bf V}_{1},\cdots,{\bf V}_{d+1}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} in general position, and let Sd:=conv​(Xd)S_{d}:=\hbox{conv}(X_{d}) be the simplex generated from the vertices Xd.X_{d}.

We note that the dimension of the polynomials of degree at most nn in dd real variables is

dim⁡(𝒫n​(ℝd))=Nn(=N):=(n+dd).{\rm dim}({\cal P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))=N_{n}(=N):={n+d\choose d}.

For a basis {p1,⋯,pN}\{p_{1},\cdots,p_{N}\} of 𝒫n​(ℝd){\cal P}_{n}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and NN points 𝐱1,⋯,𝐱N{\bf x}_{1},\cdots,{\bf x}_{N} in SdS_{d} we may form the Vandermonde determinant

vdm⁡(𝐱1,⋯,𝐱N):=det⁡([pj​(𝐱i)]1≤i,j≤N).{\rm vdm}({\bf x}_{1},\cdots,{\bf x}_{N}):={\rm det}([p_{j}({\bf x}_{i})]_{1\leq i,j\leq N}).

In case the vandermonde determinant is non-zero, the problem of interpolation at these points by polynomials of degree at most nn is regular, and we may, in particular, construct the fundamental Lagrange polynomials ℓi​(𝐱)\ell_{i}({\bf x}) of degree nn with the property that

ℓi​(𝐱j)=δi​j.\ell_{i}({\bf x}_{j})=\delta_{ij}.
Definition 0.1.

A set F⊂SdF\subset S_{d} of NN distinct points is said to a set of Fekete points of degree nn if they maximize |vdm⁡(𝐱1,⋯,𝐱N)||{\rm vdm}({\bf x}_{1},\cdots,{\bf x}_{N})| over SdN.S_{d}^{N}.

Definition 0.2.

A set F⊂SdF\subset S_{d} of NdN_{d} distinct points is said to be a Fejèr set if

max⁡∑i=1Nnx∈Sd⁡ℓi2​(x)=1.\max_{x\in S_{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{n}}\ell_{i}^{2}(x)=1.

More generally, we may consider for a probability measure

μ∈ℳ⁡(Sd):={μ:a​probability​measure​supported​on​Sd},\mu\in{\cal M}(S_{d}):=\{\mu\,:\,{\rm a\,\,probability\,\,measure\,\,supported\,\,on}\,\,S_{d}\},

the associated Gram matrix

Gn​(μ):=[∫Sdpi​(x)​pj​(x)​𝑑μ]∈ℝN×N.G_{n}(\mu):=[\int_{S_{d}}p_{i}(x)p_{j}(x)d\mu]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.
Definition 0.3.

A measure μ∈ℳ⁡(Sd)\mu\in{\cal M}(S_{d}) for which det​(Gn​(μ)CLOSE{\rm det}(G_{n}(\mu) is a maximum is said to be D-optimal.

By the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem [9] a measure is D-optimal if and only if it is G-optimal

Definition 0.4.

A measure μ∈ℳ⁡(Sd)\mu\in{\cal M}(S_{d}) for which the diagonal of the reproducing kernel

Kn​(𝐱,𝐱):=∑i=1NPi2​(𝐱)K_{n}({\bf x},{\bf x}):=\sum_{i=1}^{N}P_{i}^{2}({\bf x})

where {P1,⋯,PN}\{P_{1},\cdots,P_{N}\} is any orthonormal basis for 𝒫n​(K){\cal P}_{n}(K) with respect to the inner product induced by μ,\mu, is such that

max𝐱∈Sd⁡Kn​(𝐱)\max_{{\bf x}\in S_{d}}K_{n}({\bf x})

is a minimum, is said to be G-optimal. In which case max𝐱∈Sd⁡Kn​(𝐱)=N\max_{{\bf x}\in S_{d}}K_{n}({\bf x})=N and this maximum is attained at all points in the support of μ.\mu.

For short, we will refer to either a D-optimal or G-optimal measure as an optimal probability measure, or optimal design,for degree n.n.

The interested reader may find more about the theory of optimal designs in the monographs [8] and [6]. The asymptotics of such measures as n→∞n\to\infty is discussed in [2].

Proposition 0.5.

Consider discrete probablity measures of the form

μ=∑𝐚∈Fw𝐚​δ𝐚,w𝐚>0\mu=\sum_{{\bf a}\in F}w_{{\bf a}}\delta_{{\bf a}},\quad w_{{\bf a}}>0

supported on a set F⊂SdF\subset S_{d} of cardinality N.N. Then μ\mu is an optimal measure for degree nn if and only if it is equallly weighted, i.e., w𝐚=1/N,∀𝐚∈F,w_{{\bf a}}=1/N,\,\,\forall\,{\bf a}\in F, and FF is a Fejèr set.

Proof. For a set of cardinality NN it is easily seen that the associated Lagrange polynomials ℓ𝐚​(𝐱)/w𝐚\ell_{\bf a}({\bf x})/\sqrt{w_{{\bf a}}} are orthonormal with respect to the measure μ.\mu. Hence

Kn​(𝐱)=∑𝐚∈Fℓ𝐚2​(𝐱)w𝐚.K_{n}({\bf x})=\sum_{{\bf a}\in F}\frac{\ell_{\bf a}^{2}({\bf x})}{w_{\bf a}}.

Now suppose first that μ\mu is optimal. Then by G-optimality, for all 𝐛∈F,{\bf b}\in F,

N\displaystyle N =Kn​(𝐛)\displaystyle=K_{n}({\bf b})
=∑𝐚∈Fℓ𝐚2​(𝐛)w𝐚\displaystyle=\sum_{{\bf a}\in F}\frac{\ell_{\bf a}^{2}({\bf b})}{w_{\bf a}}
=ℓ𝐛2​(𝐛)w𝐛\displaystyle=\frac{\ell_{\bf b}^{2}({\bf b})}{w_{\bf b}}
=1w𝐛\displaystyle=\frac{1}{w_{\bf b}}

and so the measure is equally weighted with w𝐚=1/N,w_{\bf a}=1/N, ∀𝐚∈F.\forall{\bf a}\in F. Further, by G-optimality, we must also have Kn​(𝐱)≤N,K_{n}({\bf x})\leq N, 𝐱∈Sd.{\bf x}\in S_{d}. Hence

N\displaystyle N ≥Kn​(𝐱)\displaystyle\geq K_{n}({\bf x})
=N​∑𝐚∈Fℓ𝐚2​(𝐱),\displaystyle=N\sum_{{\bf a}\in F}\ell_{\bf a}^{2}({\bf x}),

i.e.,

∑𝐚∈Fℓ𝐚2​(𝐱)≤1,𝐱∈Sd\sum_{{\bf a}\in F}\ell_{\bf a}^{2}({\bf x})\leq 1,\quad{\bf x}\in S_{d}

and so FF is a Fejèr set.

Conversely suppose that FF is a Fejèr set and that

μ=1N​∑𝐚∈Fδ𝐚\mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\bf a}\in F}\delta_{{\bf a}}

is equally weighted. Then

Kn​(𝐱)=N​∑𝐚∈Fℓ𝐚2​(𝐱)≤N×1,𝐱∈SdK_{n}({\bf x})=N\sum_{{\bf a}\in F}\ell_{\bf a}^{2}({\bf x})\leq N\times 1,\quad{\bf x}\in S_{d}

and equal to NN at the points of F.F. Hence the equally weighted measure μ\mu is G-optimal. □\square

Proposition 0.6.

A set of Fejèr points FF is always also a set of Fekete points.

Proof. The equally weighted measure supported on F,F,

μ=1N​∑𝐚∈Fδ𝐚\mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{{\bf a}\in F}\delta_{{\bf a}}

is by the previous proposition G-optimal, and hence by the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem, also D-optimal, i.e., it maximizes the determinant of the Gram matrix for polynomials of degree at most nn among all probability measures. But for an equally weighted discrete measure, ν,\nu, supported on NN points 𝐱1⋯,𝐱N,{\bf x}_{1}\cdots,{\bf x}_{N}, it is easy to confirm that

Gn​(ν)=1N​Vnt​VnG_{n}(\nu)=\frac{1}{N}V_{n}^{t}V_{n}

where Vn:=[pi​(xj)]1≤i≤nV_{n}:=[p_{i}(x_{j})]_{1\leq i\leq n} is the Vandermonde matrix. Hence det⁡(Gn​(ν))=(1/NN)​(det⁡(Vn))2{\rm det}(G_{n}(\nu))=(1/N^{N})({\rm det}(V_{n}))^{2} and so maximizing the Vandermonde determinant is equivalent to maximizing the Gram matrix over all equally weighted measures supported on NN points in Sd.S_{d}. Since the measure supported on a set of Fejèr points is optimal among all probability measures, it is also best among equally weighted measures, and hence FF is also a set of Fekete points. □\square

Remark 0.7.

It is not in general true that Fekete points by themselves are always Fejèr points; see [4] for a discussion of this problem. □\square

Remark 0.8.

Since a Lagrange polynomial may be written as a ratio of Vandermonde determinants

ℓi​(𝐱)=vdm⁡(𝐱1,⋯,𝐱i−1,𝐱,𝐱i+1,⋯,𝐱N)vdm(𝐱1,𝐱2⋯,𝐱N)\ell_{i}({\bf x})=\frac{{\rm vdm}({\bf x}_{1},\cdots,{\bf x}_{i-1},{\bf x},{\bf x}_{i+1},\cdots,{\bf x}_{N})}{{\rm vdm}({\bf x}_{1},{\bf x}_{2}\cdots,{\bf x}_{N})}

it is necessarily the case that, for Fekete points, the Lagrange polynomials are bounded by 1 on SdS_{d} or, in other words,

‖ℓ⁡(𝐱)‖∞≤1,𝐱∈Sd\|{\bm{\ell}}({\bf x})\|_{\infty}\leq 1,\quad{\bf x}\in S_{d}

where

ℓ⁡(𝐱)=[ℓ1​(𝐱),⋯,ℓN​(𝐱)]∈ℝN{\bm{\ell}}({\bf x})=[\ell_{1}({\bf x}),\cdots,\ell_{N}({\bf x})]\in\mathbb{R}^{N}

denotes the vector of the Lagrange polynomials. Note however that this boundedness condition is not sufficient to be a Fekete set. Indeed, consider for degree 1 the simplex (triangle) S2S_{2} in ℝ2,\mathbb{R}^{2}, degree 1 and the three edge midpoints, (V1+V2)/2,(V_{1}+V_{2})/2, (V1+V3)/2(V_{1}+V_{3})/2 and (V2+V3)/2.(V_{2}+V_{3})/2. It is easy to confirm that the associated Lagrange polynomials are 1−2​λ3,1-2\lambda_{3}, 1−2​λ21-2\lambda_{2} and 1−2​λ1,1-2\lambda_{1}, respectively. As λj∈[0,1],\lambda_{j}\in[0,1], each of these Lagrange polynomials takes values in [−1,1],[-1,1], i.e., is bounded by 1 in absolute value. However, the three edge midpoints do not form a Fekete set, as their Vandermonde determinant is 1/2×area⁡(S2)1/2\times{\rm area}(S_{2}) whereas the Vandermonde determinant for the three vertices is 2×area⁡(S2).2\times{\rm area}(S_{2}). □\square

We will now proceed to discuss the degrees 1 through 5 situations, based on sets of points introduced in [3]. The idea is to place a maximal number of points on the boundary of the simplex in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, in such a way that restricted to a lower dimensional face of dimension 0≤d′<d0\leq d^{\prime}<d we obtain the prescribed set of points for the simplex in ℝd′.\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}}. On any edge, i.e. , a one dimensional face, we place the univariate Fekete points, which are known to be the zeros of (x2−1)​Pn′​(x),(x^{2}-1)P_{n}^{\prime}(x), where Pn​(x)P_{n}(x) is the nnth classical Legendre polynomial.

1 Degree One

For degree one the dimension of the polynomials is d+1.d+1.

Proposition 1.1.

(cf. [3]) The set F1=Xd⊂SdF_{1}=X_{d}\subset S_{d} is a set of Fejèr points of degree one for all dimensions d.d.

Proof. The Lagrange polynomial for the iith vertex ViV_{i} is just ℓi=λi,\ell_{i}=\lambda_{i}, in barycentric coordinates. Now, for x∈Sd,x\in S_{d}, λi≥0,\lambda_{i}\geq 0, 1≤i≤d+11\leq i\leq d+1 and hence

∑i=1d+1ℓi2\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{d+1}\ell_{i}^{2} =∑i=1d+1λi2\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d+1}\lambda_{i}^{2}
≤(∑i=1d+1λi)2\displaystyle\leq\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d+1}\lambda_{i}\right)^{2}
=1.\displaystyle=1.

□\square

3 Degree Three

For d≥3d\geq 3 there are no longer interior points and there is a simple algebraic procedure to verify that 1−K3≥01-K_{3}\geq 0 on the simplex. We proceed by induction. Assuming that F3F_{3} is a Fejèr set for dimension d−1d-1 one calculates 1−K31-K_{3} in homogenized form

(∑j=1d+1λj)6−K3​(𝝀)\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\lambda_{j}\Bigr)^{6}-K_{3}({\bm{\lambda}})

and then considers this on the sub-simplex with vertices

If we let μ1,⋯,μd+1\mu_{1},\cdots,\mu_{d+1} be the barycentric coordinates for the sub-simplex, then it is easy to see that

λj=μj+μd+1/(d+1),  1≤j≤d,λd+1=μd+1/(d+1).\lambda_{j}=\mu_{j}+\mu_{d+1}/(d+1),\,\,1\leq j\leq d,\quad\lambda_{d+1}=\mu_{d+1}/(d+1). (3.1)

Let H⁡(𝝁)H({\bm{\mu}}) be 1−K31-K_{3} restricted to this sub-simplex, i.e.,

H⁡(𝝁)=(∑j=1d+1λj)6−K3​(𝝀)H({\bm{\mu}})=\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\lambda_{j}\Bigr)^{6}-K_{3}({\bm{\lambda}})

with 𝝀{\bm{\lambda}} given by (3.1). It is sufficient to prove that H⁡(𝝁)≥0H({\bm{\mu}})\geq 0 for μj≥0,\mu_{j}\geq 0, 1≤j≤(d+1)1\leq j\leq(d+1) for which it is, in turn, sufficient to show that

as the term H⁡(𝝁^,0)H(\widehat{{\bm{\mu}}},0) is the restriction of HH to the face μd+1=λd+1=0\mu_{d+1}=\lambda_{d+1}=0 and hence is positive by the induction hypothesis.

For positivity it is sufficient that, for some integer r≥0,r\geq 0, all the coefficients of

(∑j=1d+1μj)r​(H⁡(𝝁)−H⁡(𝝁^,0))\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\mu_{j}\Bigr)^{r}(H({\bm{\mu}})-H(\widehat{{\bm{\mu}}},0))

are non-negative. This has been verified by means of computer algebra for degrees up to 28 with r=8r=8 for dimension d=3,d=3, r=5r=5 for d=4,d=4, r=3r=3 for d=5,6d=5,6 and r=2r=2 otherwise. Appendix A gives Matlab code using its Symbolic Toolbox for this purpose. □\square

Remark 3.2.

Multiplying a polynomial in barycentric coordinates by one in the form of ∑j=1d+1μj\sum_{j=1}^{d+1}\mu_{j} is known as degree elevation. The minimal rr necessary to have all non-negative coefficients is connected to the so-called Bernstein degree of a polynomial which is positive on a simplex. □\square

In dimension d=3d=3 we have, for the set F4,F_{4},

∑i=1Nℓi2​(𝐱)≤1,𝐱∈S3.\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell_{i}^{2}({\bf x})\leq 1,\,\,{\bf x}\in S_{3}.

The sets F4F_{4} are Fekete sets for all dimensions d=1,2,⋯.d=1,2,\cdots.

As evidence for this conjecture we can prove that for dimensions d=3,4,5,6,7d=3,4,5,6,7 the Lagrange polynomials for F4F_{4} satisfy the necessary (but not sufficient) condition that they are all bounded by 1. Indeed, somewhat more is true.

ℓi​j​k​ℓ=256​λi​λj​λk​λℓ=256​λi​λj​λk​λℓ\ell_{ijk\ell}=256\lambda_{i}\lambda_{j}\lambda_{k}\lambda_{\ell}=256\lambda_{i}\lambda_{j}\lambda_{k}\lambda_{\ell}

λj\displaystyle\lambda_{j} =μj+1d+1​μd+1,  1≤j≤d,\displaystyle=\mu_{j}+\frac{1}{d+1}\mu_{d+1},\,\,1\leq j\leq d, (4.1)

Remark 4.5.

One could of course continue this procedure dimension by dimension, but a general proof is much to be preferred. □\square

Numerical computations indicate that, at least for dimensions d=3,4,5,d=3,4,5, the sum of the fourth powers of the Lagrange polynomials is bounded by 1.

Conjecture 4.6.

For all dimensions d≥1,d\geq 1, we have

∑j=1Nℓj4​(𝐱)≤1,𝐱∈Sd\sum_{j=1}^{N}\ell_{j}^{4}({\bf x})\leq 1,\,\,{\bf x}\in S_{d}

or, in other words,

‖ℓ⁡(𝐱)‖4≤1,𝐱∈Sd.\|{\bm{\ell}}({\bf x})\|_{4}\leq 1,\,\,{\bf x}\in S_{d}.
Remark 4.7.

We use the fourth power in order to remain in the domain of polynomials. However, numerical computations indicate that there is a smaller exponent

r≈2.00217448r\approx 2.00217448

such that

∥ℓ(𝐱)∥r≤1,𝐱∈Sd,d=4,5.\|{\bm{\ell}}({\bf x})\|_{r}\leq 1,\,\,{\bf x}\in S_{d},\,\,d=4,5.

Definition 4.8.

‖ℓ⁡(𝐱)‖r≤1,𝐱∈Sd\|{\bm{\ell}}({\bf x})\|_{r}\leq 1,\,\,{\bf x}\in S_{d}

and for which for r′<r,r^{\prime}<r,

max𝐱∈Sd⁡‖ℓ⁡(𝐱)‖r′>1.\max_{{\bf x}\in S_{d}}\|{\bm{\ell}}({\bf x})\|_{r^{\prime}}>1.

□\square

We speculate that the Fekete points have minimal Fejér exponent.

5 Degree Five

For degree 5 we are able to give explicit formulas for the points on the edges but can express the points in the interior of the 2-faces only in terms of the roots of a certain polynomial. Consequently this section will be largely numerical.

We describe first the set of points F5F_{5} in ℝ2.\mathbb{R}^{2}. The dimension of the space of polynomials of degree at most five in two variables is N2=(5+22)=21.N_{2}={5+2\choose 2}=21. F5F_{5} will consist of the 3 vertices together with 4 additional points on each of the 3 edges, leaving 21-15=6 points to be placed in the interior of the triangle. The 4 interior edge points are just the interior univariate Fekete points of degree 5, i.e., the zeros of P5′​(x),P_{5}^{\prime}(x), the derivative of the Legendre polynomial of degree 5. Now

P5​(x)=18​(63​x5−70​x3+15​x)P_{5}(x)=\frac{1}{8}\bigl(63x^{5}-70x^{3}+15x\bigr)

and hence

P5′​(x)=158​(21​x4−14​x2+1)P_{5}^{\prime}(x)=\frac{15}{8}\bigl(21x^{4}-14x^{2}+1\bigr)

with zeros

z=±7±2​721z=\pm\sqrt{\frac{7\pm 2\sqrt{7}}{21}}

with barycentric coordinates

(1−z2,1+z2).\Bigr(\frac{1-z}{2},\frac{1+z}{2}\Bigr).

For the 6 interior points, we assume that these are symmetric and have barycentric coordinates

Hence the Vandermonde determinant of all 21 points will decouple into a factor depending on the boundary points (given) and the Vandermonde determinant for the 6 interior points with basis λ1​λ2​λ3​q​(𝝀)\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}\lambda_{3}q({\bm{\lambda}}) for

Remark 5.1.

Although the 6 interior points appear visually to all be on an interior triangle, close inspection of the coordinates reveals that this is not the case. □\square

Numerical Example 5.2.

For dimension d=2,d=2, the set F5F_{5} of the 21 points defined above do not form a Fejér set. Indeed,

max⁡∑i=121𝐱∈S2⁡ℓi2​(𝐱)≈1.2246\max_{{\bf x}\in S_{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{21}\ell_{i}^{2}({\bf x})\approx 1.2246

which is attained at the centroid (1/3,1/3,1/3).(1/3,1/3,1/3).

However, we do believe that they are Fekete points. Indeed it’s Fejér exponent is

r≈2.2513.r\approx 2.2513.

In particular, all the Lagrange polynomials are bounded by 1 in absolute value on S2.S_{2}. □\square

We now proceed to dimension d=3.d=3. Here the dimension of the space of polynomials of degree at most 5 is

N5=(5+33)=56.N_{5}={5+3\choose 3}=56.

The set F5F_{5} is such that restricted to any 2-face we obtain its two-dimensional version, i.e., we place 1 point at each of the 4 vertices, 4 interior points on each of the 6 edges and 6 interior points on each of the 4 2-faces, for a total of 4+4×6+6×4=524+4\times 6+6\times 4=52 boundary points. This leaves 56−52=456-52=4 points to be placed in the interior of the simplex. By symmetry we assume that these are

(1−3​w,w,w,w)\displaystyle(1-3w,w,w,w) (5.1)

are all zero on the boundary. Hence (cf. [5]) the Vandermonde determinant for the 56 points will factor into a constant (depending on the boundary points) times the Vandermonde determinant for the 4 points (5.1) with basis

Numerical Example 5.3.

There is a curious behaviour here. For both choises of w=(9±5)/38,w=(9\pm\sqrt{5})/38, the Lagrange polynomials are all bounded by one in absoliute value, i.e.,

‖ℓ⁡(𝐱)‖∞≤1,𝐱∈S3.\|{\bm{\ell}}({\bf x})\|_{\infty}\leq 1,\,\,{\bf x}\in S_{3}.

However, the choice of w=(9−5)/38w=(9-\sqrt{5})/38 produces a strictly larger Vandermonde determinant and hence only with this choice of ww can F5F_{5} be a Fekete set, which we conjecture to be the case.

It is also interesting to note that with w=(9+5)/38,w=(9+\sqrt{5})/38, the Fejér exponent is >4,>4, wheras for w=(9−5)/38,w=(9-\sqrt{5})/38, the Fejér exponent remains, as in dimension d=2,d=2,

r≈2.2513.r\approx 2.2513.

In this way we have 5 vertex points, 4 interior points on each of the (52)=10{5\choose 2}=10 edges, 6 interior points on each of the (53)=10{5\choose 3}=10 2-faces and 4 interior points on each of the (54)=5{5\choose 4}=5 3-faces, for a total of 5+4×10+6×10+4×5=1255+4\times 10+6\times 10+4\times 5=125 boundary points so that there is but 1=126−1251=126-125 to be placed in the interior of the simplex. We put this point at the centroid (1/5,1/5,1/5,1/5,1/5).(1/5,1/5,1/5,1/5,1/5).

We conjecture that the set F5F_{5} of 126 points so constructed is a Fekete set. Indeed it remains the case that the Fejér exponent is

r≈2.2513r\approx 2.2513

and so, in particular, all the Lagrange polynomials are bounded by 1 in absolute value. □\square
